written.q: Explain how a character is sent in asynchronous serial communication and why the baud rate must match at both ends.
written.a: The idle line is high. The transmitter sends a start bit (0), the data bits LSB first and a stop bit (1), so 10 bits for 8N1. There is no clock line: the receiver detects the falling edge of the start bit, then samples each bit in the middle of its bit time using its own clock. If the baud rates differ the sampling instants drift and the character is corrupted.

written.q: Compute UBRR and the baud rate error for 19 200 baud at 16 MHz, and for 115 200 baud. Comment.
written.a: 19 200: UBRR = 16 000 000/(16×19 200) − 1 = 51.08, use 51; actual = 16 000 000/(16×52) = 19 230.8; error +0.16 %. 115 200: UBRR = 7.68, use 8; actual = 16 000 000/(16×9) = 111 111; error −3.55 %, too large for reliable communication; use the double speed mode or a crystal such as 18.432 MHz.

written.q: Describe how the receive complete interrupt and the data register empty interrupt are used in the charEncloser using interrupts.
written.a: RXCIE0 is enabled. When a character arrives ISR(USART_RX_vect) stores UDR0 in the middle of the array {'[', ' ', ']'}, disables the receive interrupt and enables the UDRE interrupt. Each ISR(USART_UDRE_vect) writes the next array element to UDR0; after the third it resets the index, disables the UDRE interrupt and re-enables the receive interrupt. main() is free.

written.q: Discuss the pros and cons of using stdio functions (printf, getchar) in embedded firmware.
written.a: Pros: standard, portable, device-independent through streams (serial, LCD), convenient formatted I/O, shorter code. Cons: large flash and RAM overhead, slower and blocking, floating-point formatting needs extra libraries, less predictable timing; unsuitable on very small devices if memory is tight.
